newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir poll result seen as chance for peace.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir poll result seen as chance for peace.

text.p: A crushing electoral victory gives Kashmir's apostle of autonomy a unique chance to bring peace to the turbulent region, analysts said on Thursday.

Farooq Abdullah, leader of the regional National Conference party, swept to a landslide victory in the first assembly polls in Jammu and Kashmir state since a separatist revolt broke out nearly seven years ago.

With results declared in 81 of 87 constituencies, the National Conference had won 54 seats. Its nearest competitors, the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Congress party, lagged far behind with seven seats apiece.
Counting in the six remaining constituencies that went to the polls over the weekend was to start on Thursday.
"This is the best chance for peace," said Vinod Mehta, editor of Outlook magazine. "Farooq knows he won't get another chance. He has a genuine opportunity."

Pran Chopra, an analyst with the Centre for Policy Research, was also upbeat. "I don't think that at anytime in the past seven, eight or nine years could one have foreseen a development as welcome as this," Chopra said. "This is the best one could have hoped for."
The surprisingly wide margin of victory gives Abdullah the legitimacy and room for manoeuvre that will be needed to bring peace to the strife-torn region, analysts said.
Significantly, his party gained ground in the mostly-Hindu Jammu and Buddhist Ladakh regions, as well as in the Moslem majority Kashmir Valley.

Buoyed by an absolute majority in the state assembly, the 59-year-old Kashmiri wasted no time extending an olive branch to moderate separatists who boycotted the polls, the first since the insurgency erupted in 1990.
"He has to win back those who are not congenital haters of India," Mehta said.
The separatist All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, comprising some 30 political and religious groups, denounced the polls as a mockery of Kashmiris' longing for freedom from Indian rule.
But the Hurriyat's own divisions between hardliners and more moderate elements were exposed during the campaign when it suspended Shabir Shah, one of its less truculent members.

Shah is often called the "Nelson Mandela of Kashmir" because he, like the South African leader, spent years in jail for political convictions. Polls show Shah to be one of the state's most popular figures.

The National Conference could be expected to woo Shah as well as some members of the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front, which has adopted a more moderate stance since the revolt began, analysts said.

Abdullah was within striking distance of a two-thirds majority of 58 seats in the state legislature. That would give his party leeway to amend the state constitution to provide for greater autonomy to the Himalayan region.
The National Conference leader has called for the restoration of powers that during the past four decades the central government has progressively seized.
The cry for autonomy placed Abdullah's regional party squarely between militants calling for secession and national parties too closely associated with federal rule.
Abdullah immediately announced he wanted his party to join Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition.

"This gives Farooq's government a hold on the United Front and strengthens the United Front," a Western diplomat said. "The United Front will have an interest in seeing that the National Conference succeeds. That is a positive development."

In 1987, Abdullah threw his lot in with former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi of Congress. Historians say widespread allegations of rigging alienated many Moslem leaders, who then joined the separatist movement.
